en: *Ji gu jin fo dao lun heng* (A Collection of Weighing Treatises on Buddhism and Daoism from Antiquity to the Present), Volume Jia:
The Monk Shi [Dao’an] of Ximing Monastery of the Tang;
the Golden Man Appearing in a Dream to Emperor Ming of the Later Han; the Entry of Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna into Luoyang; and the Daoists’ Petition.
1. Seeking the Horn: An Account of Testing Matters. 2. During the Wei Dynasty, Sun Chong, the Ruler of Wu, held the Buddhist community in high esteem;

he established stupas and monasteries for the Buddha and consequently inquired about the relative superiority of the Three Teachings. Attached: "Discourse on Discerning the Way" by Cao Zhi, Prince of Chen of the Wei Dynasty.

Attached: "Treatise on Laozi Not Being a Great Sage" by Sun Sheng of the Jin Dynasty. Attached: "Questions and Counter-Interrogations Regarding Laozi" by Sun Sheng of the Jin Dynasty. Attached: [The account of] Emperor Yuanwei.
1. On the matter of how the simultaneous belief in Śākyamuni and Laozi led to periods of both prosperity and decline; 2. An account of the circumstances surrounding this; 3.
During the reign of Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty, he assembled his ministers to discuss Buddhist principles and governance, resulting in a period of great peace; 4.

When Emperor Ming of the Wei dynasty ascended the throne, he summoned śramaṇas and Daoists to debate the relative precedence of Buddhism and Daoism; 5. Emperor Gaozu of the Liang dynasty initially served the teachings of Huang-Lao.
6. Later Conversion to Buddhism and the Imperial Decree to Abandon the Worship of Laozi; 7. The Northern Qi Gaozu Wenchuan Emperor’s Imperial Decree to Abolish Daoism. 1.
Emperor Ming of the Han’s Dream of the Golden Man and the Entry of Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna into Luoyang:
The Daoist Masters Request a Contest of Powers. (A) Emperor Ming of the Han’s Dream of the Golden Man and Kāśyapa...
When Nāgārjuna entered Luò, various Daoist practitioners requested a contest of skills; this is recorded in the *Han fǎběn nèi zhuàn* (Inner Biography of the Origin of the Dharma in the Han):
"In the third year of the Yǒngpíng era of Emperor Míng, the Sovereign dreamed of a divine being with a golden body sixteen feet tall."
A sun-disk appeared above his neck and flew before the palace;
he was delighted by this and,
on the following day, questioned his ministers.
"What deity is this?
A man of broad learning, Fu Yi, replied:
Your servant has heard that in India there are those who have attained the Way,
called Buddhas; they fly through the void,
and their bodies possess the light of the sun.
"It must surely be his spirit!
Thereupon the Emperor was enlightened;
he dispatched Langzhong Cai Yin, Langjiang Qin Jing, and the scholar-disciple Wang Zun, along with seventeen others, totaling eighteen people.
In the Great Yuezhi country of Central India,
he transcribed the forty-two chapters of the Buddhist sutras and concealed them in the fourteenth chamber of the Stone Chamber at the Lan Tai.
Furthermore, he established a Buddhist monastery outside the Yong Gate to the west of the city of Luoyang.
On its walls were painted a thousand chariots and ten thousand cavalry circling the stupa three times;
furthermore, standing images of Śākyamuni were painted upon the Qingliang Terrace of Nangong and atop the Kaiyang City Gate.
He commissioned images of the Buddha for worship and constructed a mausoleum at that time,
naming it Xianjie.
Furthermore, Buddhist images were also fashioned upon it,
as extensively detailed in the works of Mouzi.
At that time, there were the śramaṇas Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna.
His station and conduct were beyond compare, and his resolve was set upon enlightening and transforming others.
Upon receiving the mission of Cai Yin, he traveled to India and requested that Dharmaratna proceed eastward.
Without restricting himself to a fixed location,
he traveled to Luoyang to explain the true nature of things to the people,
making reverence and faith his fundamental principle.
The Emperor asked Fotudeng,
"Since the Dharma King has appeared in the world,
why has his transformation not reached this place?"
Foteng said:
"Kapilavastu is the center of ten billion suns and moons within the trichiliocosm."
All Buddhas of the three periods of time are born therein.
Furthermore, all devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits who possess vows and practice are likewise born there.
Having received the Buddha’s correct transformation,
they all attained realization of the Way;
sentient beings in other places lacked the karmic conditions to move the Buddha.
The Buddha did not go there.
Although the Buddha did not go,
his radiance reached that place.
In some cases five hundred years,
in others one thousand years,
or even beyond one thousand years, there will always be sages.
He transmitted the Buddha’s teachings and transformed others through his guidance,
expounding the meaning of the doctrine extensively.
The Emperor placed great faith in and esteemed him.
On the first day of the first month of the fourteenth year of the Yongping era,
the Daoist masters of the Five Peaks and various mountains,
during their audience for the New Year, addressed one another, saying:
The Son of Heaven has abandoned our Way and Dharma to seek afar for the barbarian teachings.
Now, taking advantage of the imperial assembly, we may submit a memorial to oppose them.
The memorial reads as follows:
The disciples of the Three Caverns of the Most High, including Chu Shanxin and others from the Five Peaks and eighteen mountains, respectfully submit this memorial regarding their death penalty:
Your servant has heard that the Most High is formless, nameless, infinite, and unsurpassed; it is the void and spontaneous Great Way that emerged before the creation of all things.
In antiquity, all followed the same path, and the principles of the hundred kings remained unchanging.
Now, Your Majesty’s Way surpasses that of Fuxi and Huangdi, and your virtue exceeds that of Yao and Shun.
Yet I have heard in private that Your Majesty has abandoned the fundamental and pursued the peripheral.
He sought instruction from the Western Regions;
what he served was a barbarian deity,
and what he preached did not accord with the traditions of China.
We pray that Your Majesty will forgive our offenses and grant us the opportunity for examination.
Among the Daoist masters of our various mountains, there are many who possess the power of clairvoyance and clairaudience and are extensively versed in the classics.
Since the time of the Primordial Sovereign (Yuánhuáng),
there has been no one among the multitude of High Lords who has not thoroughly mastered and reached the ultimate depths of the talismans and incantations of the Great Void;
some even command and employ ghosts and spirits.
Some swallowed the morning mists and drank the vital breath;
some entered fire without being burned;
some walked upon water without drowning.
Some ascended to heaven in broad daylight;
others vanished from sight, their whereabouts unfathomable.
As for their mastery of esoteric arts and medicinal elixirs—
There is nothing he cannot do;
I wish to be able to compare my skills with his.
First, this would bring peace of mind to Your Majesty.
Second, one can thereby distinguish the true from the false;
third, the Great Way will have a destination;
fourth, the customs of the Middle Kingdom will not be thrown into disorder.
If our comparison proves inferior,
we submit to your further adjudication;
if it proves superior, we beg that the falsehood be removed.
An imperial edict was issued dispatching Song Xiang, Director of the Imperial Secretariat, to lead him into the Changle Palace.
The Emperor decreed that on the fifteenth day of this month,
they should assemble at Baima Monastery.
The Daoist masters then established three altars,
each with twenty-four gates.
The Daoist master of Mount Nanyue, Chu Shanxin, [was appointed].
Liu Zhengnian, a Daoist of Mount Hua;
Huan Wendu, a Daoist of Mount Heng;
and Jiao Dexin, a Daoist of Mount Dai.
There were six hundred and ninety people in total,
including the Daoist Lü Huītōng of Mount Sōng and the Daoists Qí Wénxìn and others from eighteen mountains,
such as Mount Huó, Tiānmù, Wǔtái, and Bái lù.
Each brought five hundred and ninety scrolls, including the *Lingbao Zhenwen*, the *Taishang Yujue*, and the *Sanyuan Fulü*,
which were placed upon the western altar.
There were also one hundred and thirty-five scrolls of the *Zi-shu* (Master’s Writings) from twenty-seven schools, such as those of Maoshengzi, Xuchengzi, Huangzi, and Laozi.
Place [the offerings] upon the central altar.
Prepare the sacrificial food and present it as an offering to the hundred deities.
Place [the offerings] upon the eastern altar.
At that time, the Emperor was presiding in a traveling palace located at the south gate of the monastery.
He placed the Buddha’s relics, scriptures,
and images on the west side of the road.
When the fast on the fifteenth day was concluded,
the Daoist masters and others used firewood and reeds mixed with incense from the altar to form a torch of agarwood.
They circumambulated the sutra and wept, saying:
"We, your subjects, address the Great Way of the Grand Ultimate, the Celestial Worthy of Original Commencement, and the myriad immortals and spirits.
Now, barbarians have brought chaos to the Central Lands."
"The sovereign has placed his trust in heterodoxy;
the orthodox teaching has lost its traces and the profound tradition has fallen into ruin.
We, your servants, venture to place the scriptures upon the ritual altar and employ fire as a means of verification."
Desiring to demonstrate to the multitude of minds the means of distinguishing the true from the false,
he set fire to the scriptures;
the scriptures were consumed by the flames and entirely reduced to ashes.
The Daoist masters looked at one another, their faces turning pale with great terror;
those who were about to ascend to heaven found they lacked the power to make themselves invisible,
and those who could command ghosts and spirits found their incantations went unanswered.
Each harbored feelings of shame and remorse;
the Daoist Fei Shucaí of Nanyue died out of self-reproach.
The Grand Tutor Zhang Yan said to Chu Xin,
"That which you have tested has yielded no results;
this is nothing but falsehood."
"It would be appropriate to follow the true Dharma that has come from the West. Chu Xin said,
"Mao Chengzi once remarked:"
The Most High is Lord Lingbao. That which constitutes the work of creation is called the Grand Primal (Taisu).
How could this be false?
Yan said: "The Grand Beginning (Taisu) possesses the reputation for honoring virtue, yet it has no designation for verbal instruction.
Now you speak of having verbal instruction."
This would then be a falsehood.
Believing this, he remained silent.
At that time, the light from the Buddha’s relics was five-colored.
It rose straight up into the air, revolving like a canopy,
covering the entire assembly and obscuring the sunlight.
Dharma Master Mātanga leaped upward and flew high.
Seated and reclining in mid-air, he extensively manifested miraculous transformations.
At that time, celestial flowers rained down upon the Buddha and the Sangha,
and the sound of heavenly music was heard, moving the hearts of all people.
The great assembly was moved with joy and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.
They all circumambulated Dharmarāta and requested him to expound the essential points of the Dharma.
Dharmarāta then produced a voice like that of Brahmā and praised the merits of the Buddha.
He also caused the great assembly to extol the Triple Gem and explained that all wholesome and unwholesome dharmas have their respective retributions,
and that the characteristics of the six realms and the three vehicles are not the same.
Furthermore, it is said that the merit of leaving the household life is the highest of all blessings;
the initial establishment of Buddhist temples was equal in measure to the merit of Brahma.
At that time, Liu Jun, the Minister of Works and Marquis of Yangcheng, along with over a thousand officials, scholars, and commoners, left the household life.
Furthermore, six hundred and twenty-eight people, including the Daoist masters of Mount Luohu and Mount Yue such as Lü Huītōng, entered the monastic order.
Yin Fùrén, Wáng Jiéhǎo, and two hundred and thirty other palace ladies and women likewise entered the monastic order.
From the end of the month onward, various offerings were provided daily for almsgiving;
Dharma robes and ritual vessels were all supplied by the relevant authorities,
and ten monasteries were subsequently established.
Seven monasteries were established for monks outside the city walls,
and three monasteries were established for nuns within the capital city;
thus did the Buddhist Dharma begin to flourish in Han China.
When Kāśyapa Mātanga first arrived from the West,
he brought with him a painted standing image of Śākyamuni;
the Emperor then ordered that it be reproduced as a drawing.
Offerings were made at Lingyuan and Luomen. 2.

During the Former Wei period, the Ruler of Wu revered the Buddhist community and established stupas and monasteries for the Buddha; consequently, he inquired about the relative superiority of the Three Teachings. (A) Regarding the matter of the Ruler of Wu’s inquiry into the relative superiority of the Three Teachings during the Former Wei period, when he revered the Buddhist community and established stupas and monasteries for the Buddha, the *Wu Shu* states:
In the fourth year of the Chihu era of Sun Quan,
there was a śramaṇa named Kang Senghui,
who was the eldest son of the Grand Chancellor of the kingdom of Kangju.

The divine demeanor was upright and majestic, and his travels were undertaken for the sake of transformation. At that time, the three kingdoms stood like the legs of a tripod, each monopolizing its own power and authority.
The Buddha-dharma had reached the north but had not yet spread to the southern lands.
[Kumārajīva] then desired that the Way be bestowed upon those who had not heard it, opening the teachings throughout the region south of the Yangtze.
Upon first arriving in Jianye, he erected a thatched hut, set up an image, and practiced the Way.
When the people of Wu first saw this,
they regarded it as a strange anomaly.
The officials reported this to the throne.
The Ruler of Wu asked,
"What divine manifestations does the Buddha possess?"
The Preface states:
"The Buddha’s numinous traces have been obscured for over a thousand years;
yet his physical remains and śarīra manifest themselves without fixed location."
The Ruler of Wu said, "If you obtain the śarīra, I shall establish a stūpa for it.
After twenty-one days had passed, he finally obtained the śarīra, which shone with five colors across the heavens; when cut open, it was even harder than before, and when burned, it would not ignite.
Light emerged and produced a great lotus that illuminated the palace;
the ministers and the sovereign were struck with wonder, and their faith was awakened.
Consequently, they constructed a stupa to save sentient beings and established a monastery.
Because the place where he resided was designated as the Buddha-vihāra and it was there that the teachings were first established,
it was consequently named Jianchu Monastery.
He then issued an edict inquiring of Kan Ze, the Chancellor of the Secretariat:
"From the time of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty until now,
how many years have there been?"
"Since Buddhism entered China so long ago,
for what reason did it only now reach Jiangdong?
Daize replied:
From the tenth year of Yongping, when the Buddha-dharma first arrived,
until the fourth year of Chihu,
one hundred and seventy years have passed.
In the fourteenth year of the Yongping era,
when the Daoist masters of the Five Peaks contended with Kāśyapa Mātanga in a contest of physical strength,
the Daoists were defeated.
The Daoist practitioners of Nanyue, including Chu Shixin and Fei Shucaī,
died while at the assembly, expressing regret for themselves;
their disciples returned them to be buried at Nanyue.
It was not previously disseminated among the ranks of those who have left the household life.
Later, having encountered the Han administration’s oppression and incessant warfare,
many years have passed until it has finally been able to flourish once more.
He asked again,
"Can Kong Qiu and Laozi be compared with the Buddha?
Zhe replied:
Your servant has heard that the Master Kong of Lu was a man of extraordinary talent and eminent refinement, whose sagely virtue was peerless.
The world styled him the "Uncrowned King," and he composed and expounded the Classics.
He provided instruction and encouragement throughout the Zhou teachings, transforming and edifying future generations.
The influence and grace of the teachers and scholars have moistened both the present and antiquity.

Furthermore, there were recluses such as Xu Chengzi, Yuan Yangzi, Zhuangzi, and Laozi; the various "Subsidiary Books" (Zi-shu) of these hundred schools all describe cultivating oneself for personal enjoyment and the unbridled liberation of the spirit.

To let one’s mind run wild in mountain valleys and study a return to simplicity that violates the rites of human relations and the distinctions between elders and juniors is not the way to settle the world or transform beings.
Reaching the reign of Emperor Jing of the Han dynasty,
because the meaning and substance of the *Huangzi* were considered even more profound than those of the *Laozi*,
the title was changed from "Zi" (Master) to "Jing" (Classic), and Daoxue (the School of the Way) was first established.
An imperial edict was issued commanding that both the court and the common people should all recite it.
If one were to compare the teachings of Confucius and Laozi with those of the Buddha from afar, they would indeed be far apart. Far apart they may be; yet—
The reason for this is that the teachings of the two masters, Confucius and Laozi,
model themselves upon Heaven in their regulations and applications, not daring to contravene Heaven.
The Buddhas have established their teachings;
the celestial laws are to be practiced and followed, for none dare to disobey the Buddha.
Speaking from this perspective:
"In truth, this is not a matter of comparison.

The Ruler of Wu was greatly pleased and appointed Huize as Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince; the rest is as detailed in the "Discourse on the Clarity of the Buddha" by Sengbing of the Jin and Song dynasties.
The Discourse on Distinguishing the Dao by Cáo Zǐjiàn, Prince of Chénsī of the Wèi Dynasty. Regarding the books of the immortals and the words of the Daoists:
It is said that Fu Yue ascended as the planet Jupiter in the lunar mansion Wei (Tail) and descended as Dongfang Shuo.
An Wang of Huainan was executed in Huainan,
yet it was said that he had attained the Way and ascended lightly;
Lady Gouyi died at Yunyang, yet it was said that she departed as a corpse and her coffin was empty.
How exceedingly false this is! Among those who uphold earnest discourse during the Zhongxing era,
there was one named Huan Junsan.
His writings were mostly excellent; Liu Zijun once asked him:
"If a person can truly suppress their cravings and desires, and close off their ears and eyes, could they avoid exhaustion?"
At that time, there was an old elm tree in the courtyard.
Junshan pointed to it and said, "This tree has no lustful desires, so it can endure; it has no ears or eyes, so it can remain closed."
Yet it remains parched and decayed;
thus, when Zizun claims it can be prevented from failing, he is not speaking the truth.
When Junshan cites the analogy of the elm tree, it is likewise incorrect.

As for the rest: previously, when I served as the Grand Master of Music under Wang Mang, the *Yueji* (Records of Music) stated that Emperor Wen obtained the musician Dou Gong from Lord Wen of Wei; he was one hundred and eighty years old and blind in both eyes.
The Emperor marveled at this and questioned him:
"What have you performed? He replied:
I was thirteen years old when I lost my sight.
My parents, grieving that I would not be able to serve them,
taught me to play the qin.
"I, your servant, am unable to guide [the breath] and do not know by what power longevity is attained.
Junshan discussed this, saying:
I find it quite plausible that the blind man’s exclusive practice of inward vision was aided by the fact that his spirit did not reflect outwardly.
Previously, you, Ziji, argued that inward vision is of no benefit;
now, in your discussion of Duke Dou, you immediately use his lack of outward reflection as proof.
"I have not yet seen a definitive argument on this matter.
Junshan further said,
"Among the fangshi (masters of arts) was one named Dong Zhongjun."
He was imprisoned for his crimes and feigned death for several days;
his eyes sank and worms emerged, yet he died and then returned to life.
Thereafter, one eventually dies.
That birth is inevitably followed by death is what the gentleman understands;
what need is there for further illustration?
Now, the ultimate spirit does not exceed that of heaven and earth, yet it cannot cause hibernating insects to emerge in summer or for thunder to strike in winter.
When the seasons change, things move;
when the vital energy shifts, events respond.
That Mr. Zhong was thus able to conceal his vital breath, cause his body to wither, his skin to rot, and the worms to emerge—is this not truly a great marvel?
There are such practitioners of the arts in the world.
They were all summoned by the King.
There was Gan Shi from Ganling,
and there was Zuo Ci from Lujiang.
In Yangcheng there was Xi Jian,
who was first able to practice breath cultivation and *dāoyin* (guiding and pulling), and was well-versed in the arts of the inner chamber (*fangzhong*).
Jian was skilled at warding off hunger and lived to be three hundred years old.
The reason I have collected these works in the State of Wei is truly out of fear that those of this ilk will employ craftiness and guile to deceive the masses,
and practice sorcery and depravity to delude people.
Therefore, they gathered together and prohibited [the practice].
Gan Shi was old yet possessed a youthful appearance;
all other practitioners of the arts unanimously turned to him for refuge.
However, the language therein is verbose and lacks substance;
I cannot help but harbor some suspicion regarding it.
Were it encountered by the likes of the First Emperor of Qin or Emperor Wu of Han, [it would surely have been suppressed].
They were merely the likes of Xu Fu and Luan Da.
Jie and Zhou were separated by different eras yet were equally evil;
these wicked men belonged to different generations yet were identical in their hypocrisy.
Is it truly so? Furthermore, there is a worldly report of "immortals" (rishi).
These so-called immortals are merely a species of monkeys and apes.
Is it that you, like those among the common people who have attained the Way, have been transformed into an immortal?
Now, when a pheasant enters the sea it becomes a clam;
when a swallow enters the sea it becomes a sparrow-vapor.
When they fluttered about with their wings spread wide,
even their feathers were still recognizable;
yet suddenly, they threw themselves down.
When the spirit undergoes transformation and the body changes, one then joins the ranks of turtles and turtles;
how could one still recognize the pleasures of soaring through forests and nesting in houses?
When Niu Ai was afflicted by illness and turned into a tiger, he encountered his own brother and devoured him.
If this is so, what is there to value in such transformations?
Yet they are easily deceived by commoners,
who accept their words of falsehood.
They believe the delusive doctrines;
they honor ritual to recruit those who do not submit as subjects;
and they exhaust their wealth to satisfy empty demands.
He bestowed upon him royal ranks to honor him and provided him with a secluded pavilion for his residence; yet,
through years and many harvests, there was ultimately not a single sign of efficacy.
Some perished at Shaqiu; others collapsed at Wuzuo.
Although at those times their bodies were executed and their clans exterminated, [the consequences persisted].
Such confusion is surely enough to provoke the laughter of the world.
Nevertheless, each person has their own allotted span of life and degree of physical strength;
those who cultivate themselves well bring these matters to their natural conclusion.
Those who cause toil and disturbance are halved [in their lifespan];
those who waste resources in vain meet with premature death. Is this not what is meant by this?
Prince Si of Chen was Cao Zhi,
styled Zijian.
He was the fourth son of Emperor Wu of Wei.
He was initially enfeoffed as the Prince of Dong'e Commandery,
and after his death, he was posthumously titled the Prince of Chen-si. From childhood,
he possessed the refined qualities of a jade vessel.
At the age of ten, he was able to compose literary works;
once he set pen to paper, they were complete without a single revision or alteration.
There was no worldly art or craft in which he was not thoroughly proficient.
When Han Dan Chun saw him, he was struck with awe and submission,
praising him as a "Heavenly Man."
Whenever Zhi read Buddhist scriptures,
he would invariably linger over them with deep admiration and contemplation,
regarding them as the ultimate pinnacle of the Supreme Way.
He subsequently devised the seven-tonal modulations for chanting, with their rising, falling, and intricate melodic turns;
all who recite in the world thereafter took these as their standard.
He once traveled to Mount Yushan.
Suddenly, he heard the resonance of Brahmā from the air;
it was pure, soaring, and plaintive, its sound moving the heart.
He listened alone for a long while.
Yet none among the attendants heard it.
Zhi was profoundly moved by the divine principle and further awakened to the correspondence of the Dharma.
He then admired their melodic rhythms and transcribed them as Buddhist chants (fanbei),
composing the texts and establishing the musical notations to serve as a model for future generations.
The manifestation of the Brahma-voice began with this.
The *bē* chants he transmitted consist of six sections,
as recorded in the *Fayuan ji* (Collection from the Garden of the Dharma) by the Liang dynasty monk Sengyou.
Nevertheless, when one comprehensively surveys the source of the Way and meticulously searches the records of the immortals,
one finds that while there are many strange and delusory accounts,
they ultimately revert to being mere embellishments and deceptions; this has already been sufficiently clarified by the arguments presented above.

Sun Sheng of the Jin Dynasty composed the "Treatise on the Sages and Worthies Following the Same Track" and the "Treatise on Lao Dan Not Being a Great Sage. Recently, I have obtained the opportunity for leisurely seclusion.
Thereafter, he set forth his reflections,
looking up to the profound subtlety of the ancients and examining the Great Sage upon the spiritual path.
By examining their elegance in detail and scrutinizing their conduct thoroughly,
one can almost discern the distinction between the high and the low. Indeed,
the Great Sage acted in accordance with the times.
Thus, their traces surge forth according to their causes;
the great sages follow the subtle.
Therefore, they unfold and retract together with the Great Sage.
Because their underlying causes differ,
there is a divergence between the traces of yielding and courtesy and those of the halberd and spear;
the latter is subtle and its Way is secondary.
Thus, the tracks of their withdrawal and emergence are no different;
it is just as dragons and tigers follow the wind and clouds,
or as forms and sounds correspond like echoes and shadows.
Principle is inherently natural;
it is not summoned. Therefore, the patterns on the milfoil stalks share the same omens.
Yuan Ji emerged safely from the jaws of tigers and rhinoceroses;
Yan Hui and Kong Qiu both met with misfortune,
yet they found leisurely composure amidst the turmoil of Kuang and Chen.
Emperor Yao took Heaven as his model;
Ji and Xie assisted in his transformation of the world.
Tang and Wu carried out the revolution; Yi Yin and Lü Shang extolled their achievements.
Based on this, one may employ the analogy of shadows and echoes to explain our discourse;
how could one not believe the conversation between you and me?
What is it that the great sages aspire to? They observe the images; by observing the images, they know the vessels;
by knowing the vessels, they provide for them in advance.
Good fortune and misfortune are pre-contained within it;
thus, good and bad fortune operate through form.
This is like governing and administering by responding to circumstances and engaging with the myriad regions.
In the end, one preserves ultimate good fortune; whether in extremity or prosperity, in stagnation or obstruction, the principle is one and the same.
One merely rejoices in the sublime joy of the *Yi*, which brings fulfillment through reliance upon conditions.
To admire the profound darkness yet be unable to enter it,
and to delight in tranquil stillness yet be unable to abide in it—
this is merely what I consider to be a state of inferiority and cause for concern.
As for the third type of person, the mediocre sage,
there is a distance from the Sage;
therefore, they have not yet fully realized the Way of the dark essence.
Spontaneous functioning cannot itself attain profound identity with the Dao; yet,
one who aspires to antiquity and preserves excellence fixes their lofty thoughts thereon,
admiring the pure wind and exclusively chanting of the ultimate void.
Thus, there were those who dwelt secluded in the forests like the likes of Chao Fu and Xu You,
and whose conduct and speech were as steadfast as the likes of Laozi and Pengzu.
Nor is it ignited intentionally; it is natural by principle.
Indeed, those whose forms are restless long for stillness, and those whose natures are soft cherish hardness.
They defile what they habitually practice and take comfort in what they rarely hear.
This is the common practice of the world.
Therefore, upon encountering biased and contradictory statements,
people no longer seek out the appropriate application of causes and conditions.
Having encountered such perverse and crooked arguments,
one no longer realizes the error of their own straightforwardness.
Examining the Laozi’s writings, those points that accord with the Holy Teaching are as follows:
This analogy of "replacing the great artisan's chisel" and the "webbed toes and extra fingers" is indeed paradoxical.
The teaching of the Sage is a remote and appropriate means for saving the world; it accords with the principle that "clarifying the Way is like being obscure."
How could the Six Classics ever lack instruction on emptiness and stillness, or admonitions on humility and modesty?
Confucius said,
"I transmit but do not create."
Trusting in and cherishing antiquity,
I venture to compare myself to Lao Peng;
seeking this very principle, I find it so.
Thus, the Way of Laozi and Pengzu is encompassed within the scope of the Sage’s teaching; furthermore,
these two matters are pointed out as explanations that do not contradict the truth of the words.
How can this be clarified?
How could the profound stillness of the sages not be something to be cherished?
Furthermore, from the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors downwards...
There was nothing that was not created.
Thus, the diagrams of the *Yi*, the classics, and the foundational texts were brilliantly manifest.
Dwellings, houses, and garments were established in accordance with the times and for the sake of peace.
"Does this not mean 'narrating rather than composing'?
Therefore, the *Yi* says:
